items.question:
A legal ops team at a 400-person professional services firm uses Claude to review incoming NDAs and flag unusual or non-standard clauses. All flagged items are routed directly to the general counsel. After one month, the general counsel reports receiving 30–40 escalations per week, most of which are minor deviations well within the firm's standard tolerance.

What is the MOST appropriate fix to the escalation path?

options.A: Remove the escalation step and have Claude auto-accept minor deviations, routing only anomalies it cannot classify to the general counsel.
options.B: Engage an external law firm to handle the escalated NDA reviews, freeing the general counsel for higher-value strategic work.
options.C: Add a severity-classification layer between Claude and the general counsel, routing low-risk deviations to a senior paralegal and reserving high-risk items for the general counsel.
options.D: Set a weekly cap of 10 escalations and have Claude auto-clear anything above that threshold to protect the general counsel's capacity.

items.question:
A procurement team at a global manufacturing company uses Claude to generate draft purchase orders from approved supplier quotes. Procurement officers review the Claude-generated drafts and then manually re-enter the approved data into the ERP system. The team lead wants to eliminate this double-handling.

What change would MOST directly reduce double-handling while preserving appropriate controls?

options.A: Ask Claude to format draft POs in the ERP's native XML schema so officers can copy and paste them into the system faster.
options.B: Build a connector that writes the reviewed and approved PO data from Claude's output into the ERP, triggered by the officer's approval action in the workflow.
options.C: Automate PO submission so the ERP is updated as soon as Claude generates the draft, removing the need for officer review before entry.
options.D: Route Claude-generated POs directly to the supplier after generation, bypassing the ERP to remove the manual entry step entirely.

items.question:
An actuarial team at a large insurance company uploads policyholder loss data to Claude for quarterly trend analysis. A colleague proposes replacing the manual upload with an MCP connector that gives Claude live, query-level access to the full data warehouse.

Before enabling the live connection, what is the MOST important design consideration?

options.A: Whether the data warehouse vendor provides a certified MCP integration that has been tested with Claude.
options.B: Whether the live connection introduces additional latency that would slow the quarterly analysis cycle.
options.C: Whether the analysts currently hold the data access permissions required to use a live warehouse connector.
options.D: Whether the analyst's query will pull a broader set of policyholder records into the Claude context than the specific analysis requires, creating unnecessary data access risk.

items.question:
A RevOps lead at a 12-person SaaS startup prepares a weekly pipeline review report by copying opportunity data from Salesforce into Claude each Friday. A colleague suggests setting up a Salesforce connector instead.

What is the PRIMARY workflow benefit of the connector over the manual copy-paste approach?

options.A: The connector allows Claude to write updated pipeline stages and close dates back into Salesforce after the review is complete.
options.B: A Salesforce connector lets multiple team members query the pipeline simultaneously through Claude without each needing individual Salesforce credentials.
options.C: The connector removes a manual transfer step and ensures the data Claude analyses is current at the moment of the report, reducing the risk of stale pipeline figures influencing the forecast.
options.D: The connector bypasses Salesforce's API rate limits, enabling faster bulk data retrieval for high-frequency reporting scenarios.

items.question:
A communications manager at a pharmaceutical company asks Claude to draft promotional copy for a prescription drug that includes specific efficacy claims not supported by the drug's current labelled indications. Claude declines to produce the copy as requested, citing potential regulatory risk.

What is the MOST appropriate response to this refusal in a responsible workflow design?

options.A: Rephrase the prompt to frame the efficacy claims as a fictional case study, allowing Claude to generate the language indirectly.
options.B: Treat Claude's refusal as a useful workflow signal and redirect the brief to the medical affairs team, who can assess whether the claims are supportable before any promotional copy is drafted.
options.C: Switch to a higher-tier model, which has broader content capabilities for regulated-industry enterprise customers.
options.D: Split the task: have Claude draft the promotional framework and engage a specialist copywriter to add the specific efficacy language, keeping Claude out of the regulated claim.

items.question:
A learning and development manager at a large university wants to use Claude to generate personalised learning pathway recommendations for each student based on their assessment results. The team proposes publishing Claude's recommendations directly to the student portal the moment they are generated, without any staff review step.

What is the PRIMARY concern with this design?

options.A: Students may not trust AI-generated recommendations, reducing their engagement with the learning portal.
options.B: Claude's recommendations may reflect statistical biases in the assessment data, producing inequitable pathways for certain student groups.
options.C: Without a connector to the student information system, published recommendations may become outdated as student progress changes.
options.D: Claude's recommendations will enter the student record as official learning pathways without any staff member verifying they are appropriate for the individual, creating an unreviewed consequential AI decision.

items.question:
A retail bank is evaluating two workflow designs for AI-assisted loan pre-scoring:

**Proposal P:** Claude generates a pre-score; applications above a defined threshold automatically advance to the approval stage; underwriters review only borderline cases.
**Proposal Q:** Every application goes to an underwriter who may use Claude's pre-score as one input among several.

The bank's head of credit risk argues that Proposal P creates STP for high-scoring applications. A systems architect counters that the threshold was set by a qualified actuary and constitutes a form of programmatic oversight.

Whose position is CORRECT?

options.A: The head of credit risk is correct: any lending decision that advances without underwriter review is STP on a consequential financial decision, regardless of how the threshold was set.
options.B: The architect is correct: a threshold set by a qualified professional is equivalent to delegated human oversight, and Proposal P is acceptable if the threshold is validated annually.
options.C: Neither position is fully correct; the key question is whether the bank's regulator has specifically approved this threshold-based approach.
options.D: The architect is correct for clear-pass cases: where Claude's pre-score is based on the same data an underwriter would review, the human step is redundant and Proposal P is operationally superior.

items.question: A non-profit social services organisation uses Claude to help draft 40-page government grant applications. The grants director wants the workflow to be both auditable and resilient. Which TWO features should be included in the design? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Saving each Claude-generated draft with a version tag, the staff reviewer's name, and the date of their review before submission.
options.B: Using a faster, lower-cost model tier for initial drafts to reduce preparation time for high-volume grant cycles.
options.C: Defining a documented manual procedure that staff can follow to complete grant applications without Claude when the service is unavailable close to a deadline.
options.D: Automating submission to the grant portal once Claude's draft reaches a target word count threshold.
options.E: Routing all applications through the executive director for final approval regardless of grant size, to ensure senior sign-off on every submission.

items.question: An investment bank's compliance team is building a Claude-assisted sanctions screening workflow. They want to avoid overburdening senior compliance analysts while ensuring that every screening decision is defensible in a regulatory examination. Which TWO design choices BEST balance escalation discipline and auditability? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Automating clearance of all screening matches above a defined confidence threshold with no audit record generated, to minimise processing overhead.
options.B: Setting a confidence threshold below which Claude's match output is automatically routed to a senior compliance analyst for manual review.
options.C: Routing every match, regardless of confidence, to the legal department to eliminate false-negative risk.
options.D: Logging every screening attempt — including automated clears — with a timestamp, the entity screened, and the confidence score returned by Claude.
options.E: Suppressing low-confidence matches to prevent analysts from being distracted by uncertain results.

items.question: A head of digital operations at a global retail logistics company is designing a Claude-assisted workflow to process and respond to carrier rate queries. The design must be both resilient to Claude service disruptions and defensible in the event of a carrier billing dispute. Which TWO features should be included? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A documented manual procedure for carrier rate processing that operations staff can execute if Claude is unavailable.
options.B: Automatic submission of Claude-generated rate confirmations to the carrier system immediately after generation, to minimise response turnaround time.
options.C: Automatic regeneration of Claude's response if the output falls below a minimum word-count threshold.
options.D: A log of every rate calculation produced by Claude, stored with a timestamp and the name of the operator who reviewed and approved it.
options.E: A real-time connector that writes Claude's output directly to the carrier management platform as each response is generated.

items.question:
A head of AI implementation at a 90,000-person energy utility is deploying Claude to assist with drafting regulatory compliance reports. Steps completed so far: (1) all data sources that will feed Claude have been identified and inventoried; (2) Claude has been tested on a representative sample of historical compliance reports and output quality has been confirmed as acceptable. The next phase is designing the handoff and approval process before go-live.

What should the head of AI implementation do NEXT?

options.A: Train the compliance team on effective Claude usage, including how to review drafts for accuracy and how to provide corrective feedback.
options.B: Build connectors to pull live data from the identified sources into Claude, replacing the manual data preparation step.
options.C: Define how reviewed and approved draft reports will be stored in the document management system, specifying the metadata fields — reviewer identity, date, and approval status — required for regulatory audit readiness.
options.D: Deploy Claude in a limited production pilot, monitor the first 20 live compliance reports, and use findings to design the handoff process retrospectively.

items.question:
A claims handler at a mid-size insurer uses Claude to assess property damage claims. The team lead asks the handler to define the conditions under which a Claude-assessed claim should be escalated to a senior adjuster rather than processed directly.

Which condition is MOST appropriate as an escalation trigger?

options.A: Claude takes longer than 90 seconds to return an assessment, suggesting the claim is computationally complex.
options.B: The claim involves loss categories or coverage questions outside the standard policy schedule, where Claude's training may not reflect the specific policy terms.
options.C: The claimant submits more than five supporting documents, indicating a potentially large claim volume.
options.D: Claude's response uses hedging language such as 'approximately' or 'estimated', indicating stylistic uncertainty.

items.question:
A grant coordinator at a public health non-profit relies on Claude to draft narrative sections of federal grant applications. Three weeks before a major submission deadline, Claude becomes unavailable due to a platform outage. The organisation has no documented fallback procedure.

What is the PRIMARY risk this situation reveals?

options.A: The organisation's grant applications may have been overly dependent on AI-generated language, which funders might view negatively.
options.B: The workflow has a single point of failure: the absence of a manual fallback means a temporary service disruption can cause a missed deadline on a mission-critical deliverable.
options.C: The platform outage may also affect other AI tools the organisation uses, compounding the productivity impact.
options.D: Without Claude, the grant coordinator cannot verify that previous submissions were accurate.

items.question:
A revenue analyst at a logistics company uploads monthly invoicing data to Claude for anomaly detection. In one session, the analyst uploads a file that includes three months of data rather than the current month only. Claude flags anomalies across all three months without distinguishing between them.

What does this situation PRIMARILY illustrate about handoff design?

options.A: Claude cannot reliably perform anomaly detection on large datasets and should be replaced with a dedicated analytics tool for this use case.
options.B: The analyst should use a Project knowledge document to store monthly data so Claude can access it across sessions.
options.C: The scope of the data handed off to Claude directly determines the scope of its analysis; poorly bounded input produces poorly bounded output.
options.D: Claude should be prompted to ask for clarification before performing analysis when the input data spans multiple time periods.

items.question:
A regulatory reporting team at an energy company uses Claude to draft quarterly environmental disclosures. The team lead notices that their log records the final approved document but not the Claude-generated draft or the reviewer's comments. An internal auditor asks whether the log is sufficient to demonstrate that human review occurred.

What is the CORRECT assessment?

options.A: The log is sufficient: the approved document is the output that matters, and its existence implies that a human reviewed it before approval.
options.B: The log is insufficient: without the draft and review comments, the organisation cannot demonstrate what the human actually changed or verified — the record shows a result, not a process.
options.C: The log is sufficient for internal purposes but would need to be supplemented with draft records only if the regulator specifically requests them.
options.D: The log is insufficient, but only if the approved document differs materially from Claude's draft — if they are identical, the review was clearly superficial and does not need to be recorded separately.

items.question: A technology lead at a 60-person advisory firm is evaluating whether to connect Claude to the firm's matter management system via an MCP connector. The connector would allow Claude to read open matters, deadlines, and client names during drafting sessions. The managing partner asks what governance step is MOST important before enabling the connector.

options.A: Confirming that the connector's authentication mechanism is compatible with the matter management system's SSO configuration.
options.B: Reviewing which client matters and data fields will be accessible through the connector and whether any should be excluded from Claude's context based on sensitivity or conflict-of-interest considerations.
options.C: Testing the connector's response latency to ensure it does not slow down the drafting workflow for fee-earners.
options.D: Documenting the connector integration in the firm's IT asset register and assigning a system owner.

items.question:
A customer success manager at a SaaS company uses Claude to draft account health summaries after each customer call. The summaries are then copied into the CRM. A product manager suggests auto-posting Claude's summary to the CRM immediately after each call session ends, without waiting for the CSM to review it.

What is the PRIMARY concern with the proposed change?

options.A: The CRM may not have an API endpoint that supports automated posting from Claude.
options.B: Auto-posting removes the CSM's review step, meaning inaccurate or incomplete account health summaries will enter the system of record unchecked and may affect renewal decisions downstream.
options.C: The summaries may contain personally identifiable information about contacts that should not be stored in the CRM.
options.D: CSMs may feel their professional judgement is being bypassed, reducing adoption of the AI-assisted workflow.

items.question:
An HR technology lead at a 5,000-person manufacturing company is deploying Claude to assist recruiters in drafting candidate evaluation summaries after interviews. Legal counsel advises that the company must be able to demonstrate, in an employment discrimination claim, that human judgement — not AI output — determined each hiring decision.

Which workflow design feature MOST directly supports this requirement?

options.A: Using Claude only for administrative tasks such as scheduling and offer-letter formatting, not for candidate evaluation.
options.B: Configuring Claude to output evaluation summaries in a neutral, structured format that minimises the risk of biased language.
options.C: Requiring recruiters to document their own assessment of each candidate before receiving Claude's draft, ensuring the human evaluation is recorded independently of the AI output.
options.D: Storing Claude's evaluation drafts in an auditable repository with timestamps, so the company can show what the AI produced for each candidate.

items.question:
A financial planner at a wealth management firm uses Claude to draft personalised investment commentary for client reports. When asked to produce commentary recommending a specific alternative fund with limited liquidity, Claude declines, stating the recommendation would require suitability assessment that it cannot perform.

What should the firm's workflow design specify as the correct NEXT step?

options.A: Escalate the commentary request to a licensed financial adviser who can perform a suitability assessment and produce the recommendation directly.
options.B: Revise the prompt to describe the fund recommendation as a general market observation rather than a personalised recommendation.
options.C: Use a higher-tier model, which is better equipped to reason about complex financial products and suitability requirements.
options.D: Ask Claude to produce the commentary with a disclaimer that it is not financial advice, to satisfy regulatory requirements.

items.question:
A content operations lead at a media company uses Claude to generate 500 product description drafts per week for an e-commerce partner. The lead currently reviews every draft before publication, which has become unsustainable. She wants to introduce a sampling-based review approach.

What is the MOST important criterion for designing the sampling strategy?

options.A: Review a random sample of 10% of all drafts, regardless of product category or description complexity.
options.B: Review every draft that has been processed by Claude for the first time in a new product category, and a random sample from established categories.
options.C: Concentrate sampling on outputs that differ most from a validated reference description, using a similarity score to prioritise which drafts to review.
options.D: Review all drafts involving regulated product claims (health, safety, legal), and apply a lower sampling rate to low-stakes commodity product descriptions.

items.question:
An M&A analyst at an investment bank uses Claude to summarise confidential due-diligence documents for deal team briefings. The team lead discovers that Claude's summaries occasionally include deal-identifying details — company names, transaction values — that should not appear in widely distributed briefing materials.

What is the MOST effective workflow fix?

options.A: Require the analyst to redact deal-identifying details from Claude's output before the briefing is distributed.
options.B: Add an instruction to the prompt specifying that all summaries must exclude company names, specific transaction values, and deal code names.
options.C: Restrict Claude's access to the most sensitive sections of the due-diligence documents by uploading only the sections relevant to each briefing question.
options.D: Use Claude to generate internal-only summaries and then engage the legal team to review which details can be included in the distributed version.
options.E: Switch to a higher-tier model for M&A work, as it exercises better judgement about commercially sensitive information.

items.question:
A supply chain director at a food manufacturer uses Claude to generate procurement exception reports when supplier deliveries fall outside tolerance. The current workflow sends the report to the procurement manager as a notification, and the manager has 48 hours to object before the system auto-approves the exception and adjusts the contract. The director claims this constitutes human oversight. A quality auditor disagrees.

Who is CORRECT?

options.A: The director is correct: the manager has 48 hours to review and object, which constitutes a meaningful human review window and satisfies the oversight requirement.
options.B: The auditor is correct: an opt-out notification places the burden on the human to actively prevent an automated action, rather than requiring active human approval before the action occurs.
options.C: Neither is fully correct; the adequacy of the oversight depends on whether the procurement manager actually reads the notifications within the 48-hour window.
options.D: The director is correct if the auto-approval threshold was set by a senior leader, because that delegation of authority constitutes pre-approved human oversight.

items.question:
A fraud operations lead at a fintech company uses Claude to triage incoming fraud dispute cases. During a promotional campaign, dispute volume spikes to 3× normal levels. Claude's case-triage output slows, and some analysts bypass the AI step and classify cases directly to clear the backlog. Cases handled without Claude triage are processed faster but later show a higher rate of misclassification.

What does this incident MOST clearly indicate about the workflow design?

options.A: The fintech should invest in a higher-tier model that can handle volume spikes without latency degradation.
options.B: The workflow design lacks a defined protocol for handling volume spikes, creating an ad hoc bypass that removes both AI assistance and the structured triage discipline it enforces.
options.C: Analysts should not have the ability to bypass the Claude triage step; the bypass permission itself is the design flaw.
options.D: The incident shows that Claude-assisted triage is slower than manual triage and should be re-evaluated as a productivity tool.

items.question:
A head of legal operations at a 90,000-person pharmaceutical company is designing a Claude-assisted workflow for reviewing clinical trial agreements. She proposes a review checkpoint after every paragraph Claude drafts, reasoning that more checkpoints mean more oversight. A senior counsel argues this will make the workflow slower than manual review with no quality benefit.

Who is CORRECT, and why?

options.A: The head of legal ops is correct: in a regulated clinical context, checkpoint frequency should be maximised regardless of efficiency cost.
options.B: The senior counsel is correct: the optimal checkpoint frequency is determined by where in the document the risk of error is highest, not by maximising the number of review steps.
options.C: The senior counsel is correct, but only because the workflow is for clinical trial agreements where errors are unlikely due to Claude's training on legal documents.
options.D: Both are correct in part: frequency should be maximised for novel clause types and minimised for standard boilerplate sections.

items.question: A chief of staff at a global consulting firm is designing a Claude-assisted workflow for producing client-facing market intelligence reports. The workflow involves three stages: (1) a researcher uploads source documents and asks Claude for a structured summary; (2) a senior analyst reviews the summary and approves it for narrative expansion; (3) Claude drafts the full report narrative, which a partner reviews before client delivery. Which TWO design features are MOST critical for ensuring the workflow is auditable end to end? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Storing the Claude-generated structured summary, the senior analyst's approval decision, and the approved narrative together with reviewer names and timestamps at each stage.
options.B: Using a single Claude Project for all three stages so that conversation history is automatically preserved and accessible to all participants.
options.C: Requiring the partner to provide written comments explaining any changes made to Claude's narrative draft before approving the final report.
options.D: Using a consistent prompt template for the summary step across all researchers to reduce variability in Claude's structured output.
options.E: Retaining the source documents used in Stage 1 alongside the final report, so the audit trail connects delivered content back to its primary sources.

items.question: A digital transformation lead at a 400-person logistics company has deployed a Claude-assisted freight quote workflow. An escalation path routes complex quotes to a senior pricing analyst. After 60 days, the lead reviews performance data and finds: (1) 40% of all quotes are being escalated, overwhelming the analyst; (2) escalated quotes have a 3-day average review time, compared to a 4-hour SLA for standard quotes. Which TWO actions would MOST effectively improve the escalation path design? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Introduce a severity tier between standard processing and senior-analyst escalation, routing medium-complexity quotes to a junior pricing analyst for faster resolution.
options.B: Increase the senior pricing analyst headcount to absorb the escalation volume without changing the escalation criteria.
options.C: Review and tighten the escalation criteria so that only quotes meeting genuinely high-complexity thresholds reach the senior analyst, reducing the 40% escalation rate.
options.D: Remove the escalation step entirely and allow Claude to produce final quotes for all cases, with a daily batch review by the senior analyst.
options.E: Set a maximum escalation queue size and auto-approve quotes that exceed the queue limit to protect the SLA.

items.question:
A director of clinical informatics at a hospital network is deploying a Claude-assisted workflow to help physicians draft prior-authorisation letters for specialty medications. The workflow is partially designed: (1) the physician submits a structured clinical note; (2) Claude drafts the prior-auth letter; (3) a step for physician review and sign-off is defined in the diagram but not yet specified in detail. The director is now designing the specifics of Step 3.

What should the director specify FIRST within Step 3?

options.A: The maximum time a letter may remain in the review queue before it auto-advances to the payer system.
options.B: The criteria the physician must verify in the draft — specifically, clinical accuracy, patient identifiers, and the medication dose — before the sign-off action is available.
options.C: The EHR field where the approved letter will be stored, including the metadata schema for the document record.
options.D: The escalation path if the physician is unavailable — for example, which other clinician may counter-sign on their behalf.

items.question:
An engagement director at a five-person professional services firm notices that Claude-assisted client deliverables vary widely in format — some have executive summaries and labelled sections; others arrive as unformatted prose. She wants to align outputs without prescribing how each consultant runs their personal sessions.

What is the MOST direct action she should take?

options.A: Ask each consultant to append a brief personal style note to every prompt they write.
options.B: Draft a shared prompt template specifying required sections, tone, and output structure, and distribute it to all five consultants.
options.C: Have each consultant run a second Claude session to reformat their output before sharing with clients.
options.D: Configure a shared Claude Project with a custom instruction that enforces the house format for every session.

items.question:
A clinical programme manager at a 900-bed hospital is designing a Claude pilot for administrative staff using de-identified data only. Three use cases are in scope: drafting prior-authorisation letters to insurers, summarising discharge notes for care coordinators, and writing shift-handover briefings for nursing teams.

Which criterion is MOST important when selecting the single use case to start with?

options.A: Choose the use case with the highest daily transaction volume to maximise measurable productivity gain during the pilot.
options.B: Choose the use case that vocal staff advocates have already been using informally, to guarantee strong early adoption numbers.
options.C: Choose the use case where quality failures are most easily detected and corrected before they affect downstream staff or patients.
options.D: Choose the use case with the shortest average output length, to limit the volume of AI-generated text staff must review per session.

items.question:
An insurance carrier's head of claims operations is building a business case for a Claude-assisted drafting rollout to 120 staff. Her finance sponsor asks for metrics that are credible to the finance committee and actionable for the operations team on a daily basis.

Which TWO metrics best satisfy both requirements? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Average time from claim receipt to first-draft completion, measured in minutes per claim.
options.B: Net Promoter Score of the claims team, collected six months after launch.
options.C: Total Claude prompts submitted per day across all active users.
options.D: Percentage of initial drafts passing quality review without substantive revision on first submission.
options.E: Claude licence cost expressed as a percentage of the total claims operations budget.

items.question:
A category management lead at a 200-store grocery retailer has developed a Claude workflow for weekly promotional copy. She produces twenty drafts in under two hours — previously a half-day task. Her manager wants to hand the approach to a junior team member while the lead moves to a new project. After two attempts, the junior team member's output is inconsistent and she cannot replicate the lead's results.

What is the MOST likely cause of the handover failure?

options.A: The lead's effective prompts, sequencing decisions, and quality-check criteria were never written down and exist only in her experience.
options.B: The junior team member lacks the professional seniority required to use an AI workflow at this complexity level.
options.C: Claude produces different output for different users, so identical prompts yield different results across individuals.
options.D: The workflow was built on the lead's personal account and requires IT approval before a second staff member can use it.

items.question:
A quality improvement lead at a Tier 1 automotive supplier is rolling out a Claude-assisted root-cause analysis workflow to 30 quality engineers. After three weeks, adoption is stalled at 40%. Exit interviews reveal a consistent theme: engineers fear AI-generated analyses will substitute for their professional judgement in safety-critical supplier reviews.

What is the MOST appropriate response to this resistance?

options.A: Issue a management directive making Claude usage mandatory for all root-cause analyses to overcome individual resistance.
options.B: Switch to a more capable model tier so that deeper reasoning addresses the engineers' quality concerns directly.
options.C: Reframe the tool explicitly as a drafting and evidence-organisation assistant whose outputs are always reviewed and signed off by the responsible engineer.
options.D: Discontinue the workflow and treat the resistance as evidence that Claude is a poor fit for safety-critical manufacturing environments.

items.question:
A technology transformation director at an investment bank has one analyst who independently built a highly effective Claude workflow for drafting credit-memo sections — consistently producing first drafts that require minimal revision. The director wants to scale it to the full 40-person credit team next quarter and asks the analyst to lead the rollout.

Which risk is MOST likely to derail the scaling effort if left unaddressed?

options.A: The analyst's prompts may be too long for other team members to copy verbatim, requiring simplification before wider deployment.
options.B: The bank's compliance function may require a formal vendor risk assessment before approving use at this scale.
options.C: Domain expertise in credit analysis may be unevenly distributed across the 40-person team, causing output quality to vary by individual.
options.D: The analyst may be too close to the workflow to identify the implicit decisions and edge-case assumptions that colleagues will need explicit documentation on.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs head at a mid-size pharma company is planning Claude enablement for 18 regulatory writers who will draft submission summaries. Writers range from technically confident to openly sceptical. The head wants an approach that builds consistent baseline competency while accommodating the skill gap within a constrained timeline.

Which TWO enablement elements are MOST effective at achieving both goals? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Require all 18 writers to complete a three-hour self-paced e-learning module covering Claude fundamentals before first tool use.
options.B: Designate two confident writers as internal champions who facilitate peer coaching and field questions in a shared channel.
options.C: Run a live workshop using actual submission-summary drafting tasks so writers practise prompting in the context of their real work.
options.D: Provide a written acceptable-use policy and require all writers to sign an acknowledgement before tool access.
options.E: Commission a vendor to build a locked Claude interface with pre-built prompts that writers cannot modify, ensuring output consistency.

items.question:
A research computing director at a large public university oversees eight data analysts who use Claude to draft data-management plan sections for grant applications. Each analyst has developed personal prompt habits, and the resulting sections vary enough that the grants office has raised concerns about inconsistent quality across submissions.

What is the PRIMARY benefit of standardising the team on a shared prompt template for this task?

options.A: All data-management plan sections start from the same structural scaffold and tone, reducing variation without requiring analysts to change their broader personal workflows.
options.B: The university gains a platform-level audit trail of each analyst's usage, satisfying research-compliance reporting requirements.
options.C: Claude will not produce incorrect content because the template constrains the model to within an approved output space.
options.D: The grants office no longer needs to review sections before submission since standardised prompts produce reliably correct outputs.

items.question:
A freight dispatch manager at a mid-size logistics operator rolls out a Claude workflow for drafting carrier performance notifications. After six weeks he observes that new hires trained only on written SOPs take four weeks to reach productive proficiency, while those who received direct peer coaching from a senior colleague reach it in two weeks. The team is growing quickly and the manager cannot personally coach every new hire.

What training design change would MOST efficiently close this ramp-time gap at scale?

options.A: Extend the written SOP to thirty pages to ensure all edge cases are covered in enough depth for self-directed learning.
options.B: Require new hires to shadow a senior colleague for two full weeks before any independent use of the workflow.
options.C: Replace the written SOP with a vendor-provided e-learning module covering general Claude usage principles.
options.D: Embed annotated sample prompts and before-and-after output examples for the five most common notification types directly inside the existing SOP.

items.question:
A digital transformation programme manager at a city council has rolled out Claude to 60 staff across five departments for drafting public consultations and internal policy briefs. After two months, two departments are using Claude extensively with strong results. Three departments have effectively not adopted it, with staff saying the tool 'is not relevant to what we do.'

What is the MOST effective next step to address the adoption gap?

options.A: Issue a council-wide policy requiring all departments to log a minimum number of Claude sessions per week and report usage to IT.
options.B: Have the two high-adoption departments share specific worked examples from their actual council work with the three lagging departments, facilitated by a peer champion.
options.C: Upgrade the tool plan to a higher tier so that the broader feature set addresses the relevance concern.
options.D: Commission an external consultant to assess whether Claude is the right tool for the three departments' specific workflows.

items.question:
A digital advertising director at a media group ran a six-month Claude pilot for her eight-person copy team. She tracked time-per-ad-unit and first-pass approval rates before and after — both metrics improved significantly. When she presents the ROI case to the CFO, he pushes back: headcount has not decreased and ad revenue is unchanged, so he cannot see where the value went.

What is the MOST likely explanation for the CFO's scepticism?

options.A: The productivity metrics were measured incorrectly because the director did not account for time spent writing prompts.
options.B: The CFO is applying an incorrect ROI model because headcount reduction is not the only valid form of AI value.
options.C: The operational gains were real but were absorbed into higher output volume or quality rather than converted into a P&L-visible financial outcome.
options.D: The pilot lacked a control group, so the director cannot demonstrate that Claude — rather than other factors — caused the improvement.

items.question:
A patient access VP at a hospital network completed Phase 1 of a Claude pilot: five access coordinators used Claude to draft appointment-confirmation messages for complex specialty referrals over four weeks. Coordinators report good output quality and prompt iteration has stabilised. The VP now plans Phase 2: add 25 more coordinators and three new message types simultaneously.

What should the VP do FIRST before executing the Phase 2 plan as written?

options.A: Narrow the Phase 2 scope to either the additional coordinators or the new message types — but not both simultaneously — to isolate variables and maintain learning quality.
options.B: Conduct a full security review of the tool before expanding the user count, as a larger user base increases data-exposure risk.
options.C: Replace Phase 2 with a full department-wide rollout, since Phase 1 results justify skipping the intermediate step entirely.
options.D: Collect a formal satisfaction survey from Phase 1 coordinators before proceeding, as qualitative satisfaction data is required before any expansion.

items.question:
An executive director at a small environmental non-profit is the only staff member who uses Claude fluently. She has built effective prompts for grant narrative sections. The programme associate has tried using Claude independently but produces uneven results. The executive director wants to bring the associate up to speed quickly with no more than two hours of effort on either side.

What is the MOST time-efficient approach?

options.A: Send the associate links to Anthropic's public documentation so she can self-study Claude's capabilities at her own pace.
options.B: Schedule a live session where the executive director explains prompting theory while demonstrating grant-writing principles.
options.C: Set up a shared Claude Project with custom instructions and add the associate as a collaborator for persistent access.
options.D: Share the executive director's working prompt templates along with brief notes on when and how to use each, then have the associate practise on one real grant section.

items.question:
A customer operations VP at a major telecom carrier is scaling a Claude-assisted complaints-drafting workflow from a three-person pilot team to all 200 agents in the contact centre. The pilot team developed highly refined prompts over four months. Initial scaling shows new agents producing drafts that miss the empathetic tone required by the company's service charter.

Which TWO actions would MOST effectively close the quality gap for new agents? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Embed representative tone examples — showing acceptable and unacceptable draft language — as few-shot examples inside the shared prompt template.
options.B: Switch all 200 agents to a more capable model tier so the deeper language understanding produces more empathetic output by default.
options.C: Implement a quality-review gate where a team leader reviews every draft before it reaches the customer, with corrective coaching tied to specific tone errors.
options.D: Record a short walkthrough video in which a pilot-team agent narrates her prompting decisions on a real complaints scenario, and make it mandatory pre-access viewing.
options.E: Update the Project custom instructions to include the service-charter tone principles verbatim, and verify all agents access Claude through the shared Project.

items.question:
A compliance manager at an offshore energy operator introduced a Claude-assisted workflow eight months ago for drafting safety observation reports. Despite training and a champion programme, output quality has not improved beyond baseline levels, supervisor review burden has increased, and only 15% of technicians continue to use it voluntarily.

What is the MOST appropriate course of action?

options.A: Continue the programme for another six months with enhanced training, as eight months is insufficient for a complex safety reporting workflow to reach maturity.
options.B: Formally sunset the workflow, conduct a structured post-mortem to extract lessons, and redeploy the effort to a better-fit use case.
options.C: Make the workflow mandatory for all technicians so adoption numbers improve and the programme can demonstrate impact to leadership.
options.D: Escalate to IT to investigate whether a technical configuration issue is causing the quality plateau before taking any structural action.

items.question:
An operations director at a department store group rolls out a Claude-assisted store operations reporting workflow to 40 regional managers. After the launch communication, she receives an unexpected volume of concern that 'head office is going to use AI to monitor their performance more closely.' No such monitoring programme exists.

What is the PRIMARY root cause of this perception?

options.A: The regional managers are broadly resistant to any AI tool, and the director should issue a clarifying policy statement and proceed with rollout.
options.B: The AI tool was introduced alongside other management initiatives, creating confusion about which initiative is responsible for the surveillance concern.
options.C: The rollout communication emphasised the tool's capabilities but did not address what data generated in sessions would and would not be used for, leaving an information vacuum that staff filled with anxiety.
options.D: Regional managers lack sufficient technical literacy to understand how Claude works, and a technology briefing should be scheduled before continuing.

items.question:
A proposals lead at an aerospace manufacturer manages six bid writers producing technical proposal sections for government contracts. She notices that different writers use very different approaches when asking Claude to structure executive summaries, resulting in inconsistent win themes and non-uniform lengths across bids. She wants all writers to produce compliant, consistent executive summaries without constraining their domain expertise.

What is the FIRST step the proposals lead should take?

options.A: Draft a single shared prompt template for executive summaries specifying required win themes, mandatory sections, and target length range, then distribute it to all six writers.
options.B: Hold a workshop where writers share their individual prompts and the group votes on which approach to adopt as the team standard.
options.C: Ask the bid director to issue a formal policy document specifying executive summary requirements, which writers can use to self-correct their prompts.
options.D: Subscribe to a prompt-engineering training course so all writers develop equivalent personal prompting skills over time.

items.question:
A portfolio operations VP at a private equity firm rolls out Claude across eight portfolio companies for a six-month period. Her team tracked usage statistics — number of sessions, documents generated, and user satisfaction scores — and all three metrics are positive. When she presents to the investment committee, they remain unconvinced and ask for evidence of enterprise value creation.

What is the MOST accurate diagnosis of why the committee is unconvinced?

options.A: Satisfaction scores are self-reported and unreliable as evidence for an investment committee that requires third-party validated data.
options.B: Six months is too short a measurement window; the committee needs 12 to 18 months of data before drawing ROI conclusions.
options.C: The committee is applying an inappropriately strict standard by expecting AI investments to demonstrate ROI at the same speed as operational investments.
options.D: The metrics tracked measure activity and sentiment rather than financial or operational outcomes, so the programme cannot demonstrate a connection between Claude use and any value that matters to investors.

items.question:
An academic VP at a community college rolls out Claude to 120 faculty for course-design tasks: drafting rubrics, assignment briefs, and outlines. After three months, 30 faculty are active users, 70 have not logged in since onboarding, and 20 are actively negative about AI in teaching. The VP wants to move the programme forward without amplifying the sceptics' concerns.

What is the MOST effective approach to increase adoption among the 70 inactive faculty?

options.A: Issue a dean's memo framing Claude use as an institutional expectation for course-design efficiency across all departments.
options.B: Have three or four early adopters present specific course-design tasks they completed, showing actual prompts and outputs, in a peer-facilitated faculty session.
options.C: Lower the access barrier by embedding Claude directly into the college's existing learning management system to remove the separate login step.
options.D: Focus all remaining resources on converting the 20 active sceptics first, since changing their minds will have the largest impact on institutional perception.

items.question:
A training lead at a mid-tier insurance managing general agent is designing a Claude enablement programme for 35 underwriting assistants who will draft submission intake summaries and declination letters. She has a four-week window and budget covering four hours of instructor-led time per cohort. She wants the programme to produce measurable competency, not just awareness.

Which TWO programme elements would MOST effectively produce measurable competency within these constraints? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A ninety-minute classroom session explaining Claude's underlying architecture and training methodology to give assistants a conceptual grounding.
options.B: Weekly fifteen-minute stand-ups where assistants share one prompt that worked well and one that did not, building a communal prompt library over the four weeks.
options.C: A structured two-hour hands-on lab where assistants draft actual submission summaries using a template, receive scored feedback on two rounds of output, and iterate.
options.D: A post-programme scored competency assessment using representative submission-summary scenarios, with individual feedback on gaps before independent tool access is granted.
options.E: A reference card listing the ten most common prompting mistakes underwriting assistants make, distributed at the end of onboarding.

items.question:
A regulatory writer at a pharma company has developed an effective Claude workflow for producing Module 2 clinical overview sections. Her manager needs to create documentation so two additional writers can adopt the approach during a surge period. The original writer has one hour to contribute.

Which artefact produced in that hour would be MOST useful to the two new writers?

options.A: A step-by-step runbook showing the specific prompts used, the order they are applied, how outputs from each step feed the next, and the quality checks applied at each stage.
options.B: A conceptual overview document explaining why Claude is appropriate for regulatory writing and the principles behind effective prompting.
options.C: An email from the regulatory writing head endorsing the workflow and asking all writers to adopt it.
options.D: A meeting invitation for the two new writers to shadow the original writer over two full days before attempting the workflow independently.

items.question:
A VP of strategy at a third-party logistics firm wants to pilot Claude for three use cases: drafting carrier contracts, producing weekly lane-performance summaries from a structured data export, and summarising escalated customer complaint threads for the account management team. She wants the single use case that will generate the clearest, fastest quality signal.

Which use case is the BEST pilot candidate?

options.A: Carrier contract drafting, because the legal team reviews every draft, providing high-quality structured feedback during the pilot.
options.B: Lane-performance summaries from the structured data export, because output correctness is objectively verifiable against the source data and weekly volume enables rapid iteration.
options.C: Customer complaint summarisation, because complaint volume is high and the account team's daily review provides a natural feedback loop.
options.D: All three simultaneously in a parallel pilot, so the firm can compare use case performance within the same time window.

items.question:
A managing partner at a boutique strategy consultancy standardised her team on a shared Claude prompt template for client situation summaries three months ago. Structural quality has improved, but summaries now feel generic — clients occasionally comment that the content 'could apply to any company in our sector.' Consultants report using the template as written, with minimal additions.

What is the MOST likely root cause of the generic-output problem?

options.A: The template is too long, causing consultants to edit it down before sending and inadvertently removing the sections that demand client-specific detail.
options.B: Consultants are experienced writers who resist template compliance and are privately bypassing the customisation sections.
options.C: Claude defaults to sector-level patterns when generating content and cannot incorporate client-specific nuance without being fine-tuned on the client's proprietary documents.
options.D: The template lacks explicit required-fill placeholders that signal to consultants they must insert client-specific context, so they treat it as a complete prompt rather than a scaffold.
